author: moxious
cardQuote: These cars are overhyped. They've been just around the corner for the last 10 years. They are the Duke Nukem Forever of Silicon Valley.
quote: There is a difference between "trying to deal with" and "product on sale next month". These cars are overhyped. They've been just around the corner for the last 10 years. They are the Duke Nukem Forever of Silicon Valley.
outcome: Waymo One launched commercially in 2018; by mid-2026 it was running 500,000 paid rides a week across 10 metros.
outcomeDetail: Waymo began public rider-only service in Phoenix in 2018 and expanded to San Francisco, Los Angeles, Austin and other cities. By June 2026 it had 3,871 robotaxis, 500,000 paid rides per week and 200 million fully autonomous miles. The "product on sale next month" arrived, just not on the schedule critics expected.
note: moxious was right that the hype outran the product for years. He was wrong that the technology was vaporware: Waymo became the first company to run a large-scale paid robotaxi service in the U.S.

author: tintin
cardQuote: I still think it won't succeed. Electric cars have been build since 1904. But range have always been a problem.
quote: I still think it won't succeed. Electric cars have been build since 1904. But range have always been a problem. Ofcourse charging your car becomes quicker. But I still think a lot of people won't buy an electric car because they are afraid of not getting home.
storyTitle: Tesla Model S Options and Pricing
outcome: Tesla delivered 1.81 million vehicles in 2023 and has been the world's most valuable automaker since 2020.
outcomeDetail: The Model S went on sale in 2012 and became the first electric car to top the U.S. luxury sedan market. Tesla followed with the Model 3 and Model Y, built factories on three continents, and delivered 1.81 million vehicles in 2023. Range anxiety remained a real issue, but it did not stop the company from scaling.
note: tintin was right that range anxiety would slow adoption. He was wrong that it would prevent Tesla from succeeding; the Model S and Model 3 created the modern EV market.

author: ForHackernews
cardQuote: Is 'Starship' even a real thing? Last I heard, it was an empty stainless steel can ('aerodynamic model') that blew over in a strong wind.
quote: Is 'Starship' even a real thing? Last I heard, it was an empty stainless steel can ('aerodynamic model') that blew over in a strong wind. Has that changed? Are they actually going to try and make this a real launch vehicle?
outcome: Starship has flown 14 times, including flights that reached orbital velocity and catches of the Super Heavy booster.
outcomeDetail: SpaceX moved from early pressure-test failures to a series of integrated flight tests. Starship reached orbital velocity in March 2024, and Super Heavy was caught by the launch tower in October 2024. By September 2026 the program had logged 14 launches, nine of them successful.
note: The "empty can" became the largest and most powerful rocket ever flown. The comment was a fair jab at early prototypes, but wrong about the program's trajectory.

author: leesec
cardQuote: This is a cheap way to for Amazon to get into SDC, same way with their investment in Rivian. Neither have much of a shot but it's worth it to try if you're Amazon
quote: This is a cheap way to for Amazon to get into SDC, same way with their investment in Rivian. Neither have much of a shot but it's worth it to try if you're Amazon
outcome: Rivian IPO'd in November 2021, raising $13.5B; Amazon ordered 100,000 electric delivery vans.
outcomeDetail: Rivian delivered its first R1T pickups in late 2021 and began building Amazon EDVs at scale. The company went public in November 2021 in the largest IPO of the year, raising $13.5 billion. Amazon's 100,000-van order became one of the largest EV fleet commitments in the world.
note: leesec lumped Rivian in with Zoox as a long-shot Amazon hedge. Rivian became a public automaker with a real production line and a fleet customer, though it has had a bumpy financial ride since.

author: rabbitonrails
cardQuote: Tanzania launches the world's largest 2015/16 drone-hype VC funding delivery service
quote: Tanzania launches the world's largest 2015/16 drone-hype VC funding delivery service
storyTitle: Tanzania becomes the latest country to use Zipline drones for medical deliveries
outcome: Zipline passed two million commercial drone deliveries and 120 million flight miles by January 2026.
outcomeDetail: Zipline began blood deliveries in Rwanda in 2016 and expanded to Ghana, Nigeria, Kenya, Japan and the U.S. By January 2026 its drones had completed more than two million commercial deliveries and flown over 120 million miles. The Tanzania program became part of a multi-country medical logistics network.
note: The "drone-hype" jab was funny and partly fair about the 2015-16 funding cycle. It missed that Zipline would turn the demo into routine, paid medical delivery at national scale.

author: baybal2
cardQuote: It doesn't seem that the drone in question exist in anything, but CGI at the moment.
quote: Single rotor controls are much, much simpler. At least it does not require a mandatory PID control to not fall out of the sky. Very little math involved in control of a helicopter. A 3 actuator type with 1 actuator for each axis basically has no need for any control signal manipulation, and can be made fully analog. And a helicopter can be made more or less statically stable by pure mechanics, and aerodynamics. P.S. It doesn't seem that the drone in question exist in anything, but CGI at the moment. P.P.S. And quite unsound CG at that. On some of their CG shots, a swashplate actuators are attached with their axis coincidal with that rotor..., and a tail rotor control yoke not attached to anything...
storyTitle: China made the best drones, now Anduril does
outcome: Anduril's Ghost 4 entered service and the company was valued at $61B in a May 2026 Series H.
outcomeDetail: Anduril's Ghost 4 was a real, deployed autonomous drone, not a render. The company supplied U.S. and allied defense agencies and raised a $5 billion Series H in May 2026 at a $61 billion valuation. Its Lattice software and counter-drone systems are used across several Pentagon programs.
note: baybal2 read the CGI-looking marketing as proof the product did not exist. The hardware shipped and Anduril became one of the most valuable defense startups in the world.

author: anovikov
cardQuote: I wonder why are the investors pouring money into this. It is so obvious it can't work.
quote: I wonder why are the investors pouring money into this. It is so obvious it can't work. Are they simply fooled, like those guys who invested into scientifically impossible power-over-ultrasound startup? I know venture investment is risky, but is there any limit on how stupid VC partners can be? Can banks who lended them money, sue them?
storyTitle: Boom Supersonic raises $33M to build the fastest airplane for passenger flight
outcome: Boom's XB-1 broke the sound barrier in January 2025; United and American hold Overture purchase agreements.
outcomeDetail: Boom flew the XB-1 demonstrator in 2024 and broke the sound barrier on January 28, 2025, the first independently developed supersonic jet to do so. United Airlines and American Airlines have announced conditional orders for the Overture airliner. The full-size Overture has not yet flown.
note: anovikov was right that the original $33M was nowhere near enough to field an airliner. He was wrong that the physics made the project obviously impossible; the XB-1 proved the core supersonic design.

author: theon144
cardQuote: What Neuralink proposes is so far ahead in terms of what we even glimpse to be technologically possible I have trouble thinking it's not basically his pet project
quote: > Sure, it's not like a Musk company ever broke the mold before. Well to be fair they really haven't much, as far as technological advancements are concerned. Reusable rockets weren't used before not because we didn't know how to do it, but because it doesn't seem to be economical. The judge is still out on whether SpaceX will actually be able to reuse the first stages in a way that's even remotely useful. And there's even less innovation involved in Tesla cars. The only new thing they bring to the table is Autopilot, which arguably is a huge accomplishment, but not one that's "breaking the mold" in the hypercompetitive autonomous car space right now, and hasn't really delivered on its promises either. What Neuralink proposes is so far ahead in terms of what we even glimpse to be technologically possible I have trouble thinking it's not basically his pet project that is guaranteed to receive press and funding just because the topic is sexy and it has Musk's name of it. If we are ever to get as far as NL implies, it will take more than a single consumer electronics company. tl;dr I'll believe it when I see it.
outcome: Neuralink implanted its first human in January 2024 and reported 21 trial participants by January 2026.
outcomeDetail: Neuralink received FDA breakthrough designation and began its PRIME trial in 2023. Noland Arbaugh received the first implant in January 2024 and used it to control a computer and play games. By late 2026 the company reported more than 20 participants, though the device remains investigational.
note: theon144 was right that the consumer telepathy pitch was far ahead of the science. He was wrong that the implant would remain a press-release project; human trials started within five years.

author: tsimionescu
cardQuote: And if federal funds dry up, I expect the whole venture will quickly go bankrupt, or remain alive with a handful of satellites and a huge price spike.
quote: > Starlink has like 1700 of the planned 42,000 satellites in orbit now. I'm not sure if anyone believes that 42k number. They are launching ~60 satellites at a time - that would mean ~700 launches. There is no way that will be economical for the relative handful of people (500k? 1-2M?) who could realistically be interested in this. Not to mention, the lifespan of these satellites in orbit is tiny, just a few years. They would have to be constantly launching new satellites to keep up. The current state is probably more or less the best Starlink will ever offer - as more people will join the network, coming closer to Musk's 500k number, bandwidth will significantly diminish, even if the number of satellites is maybe doubled. And if federal funds dry up, I expect the whole venture will quickly go bankrupt, or remain alive with a handful of satellites and a huge price spike.
outcome: Starlink reached 13.6 million consumer subscribers by September 30, 2026.
outcomeDetail: Starlink kept launching, cut terminal costs and signed airlines, cruise lines and governments. By September 2026 it reported 13.6 million consumer subscribers and about 11,150 satellites in orbit. It became SpaceX's main revenue engine rather than a bankruptcy risk.
note: tsimionescu correctly identified the capital intensity and the risk of bandwidth dilution. He badly underestimated the demand curve and SpaceX's ability to keep lowering launch costs.

author: xphilter
cardQuote: My scam meeter is off the charts. It's exactly like Tesla except no tangible product, no funding, no founder with a proven track record, and way too many details.
quote: My scam meeter is off the charts. It's exactly like Tesla except no tangible product, no funding, no founder with a proven track record, and way too many details.
outcome: Nikola went public in 2020, then collapsed into Chapter 11 in February 2025; founder Trevor Milton was convicted of fraud.
outcomeDetail: Nikola listed via SPAC in June 2020 and briefly reached a $30 billion-plus valuation. Hindenburg Research published a fraud report in September 2020, and founder Trevor Milton was convicted of securities fraud in 2023. The company filed for Chapter 11 in February 2025 and sold its assets.
note: xphilter's "scam meeter" was exactly right: the render-heavy pitch, the missing funding and the borrowed Tesla name were all warning signs. The details that looked like proof of seriousness were part of the con.

author: rikeanimer
cardQuote: Lilium is vaporware. Ask anyone who has worked in the space. Or just look at it. Or their promotional materials.
quote: This paper "Electric VTOL Configurations Comparison" [ https://www.mdpi.com/2226-4310/6/3/26/pdf ] presents a pretty decent energetic analysis of a few of these eVTOL projects (including Lilium) and is very generous to them. Lilium is vaporware. Ask anyone who has worked in the space. Or just look at it. Or their promotional materials. Ducted fans huh... meh. I don't think they have an interest in people understand how fly-y/hover-y things actually work. I do applaud the investors for their vigorous desire to increase the velocity of money throughout society, it is important econometrically. Somehow I doubt they'll be happy to see their currency shredded by 36 rc brushless motors struggling to thrust an anemic wing into the sky though (before its glorious ~250km/h cruise to destination [of course])--and then ~15s landing hover. What exciting times to fly in.
outcome: Lilium filed for insolvency in October 2024 and ceased operations in December 2024 without delivering an aircraft.
outcomeDetail: Lilium went public via SPAC in 2021 at a $3.3 billion valuation but never certified the Lilium Jet. After the German parliament rejected a €50 million loan guarantee, the company filed for insolvency on October 24, 2024. It ceased operations on December 20, 2024 and laid off about 1,000 workers.
note: rikeanimer's "vaporware" call was blunt but accurate. The ducted-fan design and the battery assumptions never converged into a certified, deliverable aircraft.

author: marvin
cardQuote: This is not going to happen. It is a very rich, successful engineer musing at what might be possible if we thought radically different about transportation.
quote: This is not going to happen. It is a very rich, successful engineer musing at what might be possible if we thought radically different about transportation. I'm as big a fan of Elon Musk's projects as anyone, but the weight assigned to these napkin calculations is ridiculous. [Edit: If anything, this might lead people to take this type of eccentric and radical design more seriously. But given the criticism Musk's engineering ventures have had before, I wouldn't count on it.]
outcome: Hyperloop One raised more than $450M, never won a commercial route, and shut down in December 2023.
outcomeDetail: Hyperloop One built a 500-meter test track outside Las Vegas and raised over $450 million. It never signed a paying commercial route or opened a commercial service. The company laid off most of its staff and shut down in December 2023.
note: marvin's "napkin calculations" line held up: the concept never crossed from a white paper to a financed, certified transport system. The critique was right about the business, though it undersold how much money would be burned trying.

author: danbst
cardQuote: LauncherOne costs $12 millions per launch and delivers 300 kg, which means $40k/kg. Compared to $4k/kg of Falcon9, this is... uhm...
quote: LauncherOne costs $12 millions per launch and delivers 300 kg, which means $40k/kg. Compared to $4k/kg of Falcon9, this is... uhm... They definitely gotta optimize things
storyTitle: Virgin Orbit confirms that LauncherOne has reached orbit
outcome: Virgin Orbit filed Chapter 11 in April 2023 and sold its assets after failing to secure funding.
outcomeDetail: LauncherOne reached orbit in January 2021, but the economics never improved enough to sustain the company. A January 2023 launch failure from Cornwall led to a funding crisis. Virgin Orbit filed for Chapter 11 on April 4, 2023 and sold its assets, including the "Cosmic Girl" 747.
note: danbst's per-kilogram math was the whole story. Virgin Orbit could reach orbit but could not compete with Falcon 9 rideshare prices, and the market did not support a dedicated small launcher at that cost.

author: tpmx
cardQuote: There are many examples in the past where commodity manufacturing projects have eventually failed badly against Asian competitors with dramatically lower employee costs.
quote: With the quite high factory worker manpower cost here in Sweden I was (maybe still am) a bit skeptical against this commodity play. There are many examples in the past where commodity manufacturing projects have eventually failed badly against Asian competitors with dramatically lower employee costs. (Heck, even specifically in the battery space.) As I understand it, in the short term the primary motivation is providing battery volumes at a steady/guaranteed rate to their European car industry investors since there currently is a lack of stable global supply. Hard to argue against this. In the longer term, I'm guessing Northvolt is gambling that co2-neutral manufacturing of batteries will become an important enough differentiator - either by customer choice or EU legislation - that they'll be able to sell their batteries at what might end up being a relatively high premium.
storyTitle: Sweden’s Northvolt raises $2.8B to supercharge EV battery output
outcome: Northvolt filed Chapter 11 in November 2024 and Swedish bankruptcy in March 2025.
outcomeDetail: Northvolt raised billions to build European battery capacity but struggled with production ramp, quality and cash. It filed for Chapter 11 in the U.S. on November 21, 2024 and for bankruptcy in Sweden on March 12, 2025. It was the largest bankruptcy in modern Swedish industrial history.
note: tpmx was right that high-cost European commodity manufacturing would struggle against Asian battery giants. The CO2-neutral premium never arrived fast enough to cover the cost gap.

author: reTensor
cardQuote: Cruise is a mess internally. The product is unreliable garbage.
quote: Cruise is a mess internally. The product is unreliable garbage. For more details, see this recent whisteleblower account of the situation: Cruise robotaxi service under review following anonymous letter ( https://techcrunch.com/2022/07/14/cruise-robotaxi-under-revi... ) I work directly with the employee who submitted the complaint. He is understating the problem. The letter also states that Cruise ... intentionally hides from the majority of employees the results of investigations into collisions involving Cruise vehicles and other sensitive, potentially damaging matters. Cruise has been covering up safety incidents since before the GM acquisition, including an early incident where an engineer suffered a concussion due to violent cabin motion caused by bad motion control code.
storyTitle: Cruise driverless vehicles involved in 3 separate traffic incidents in SF
outcome: California suspended Cruise's driverless permits in October 2023; GM stopped funding the robotaxi unit in December 2024.
outcomeDetail: Cruise operated driverless robotaxis in San Francisco, but incidents piled up. On October 2, 2023, one of its cars dragged a pedestrian about 20 feet, and California suspended its permits. GM stopped funding Cruise's robotaxi work in December 2024 after spending roughly $10 billion.
note: reTensor's anonymous-source account of internal dysfunction was prescient. The safety culture and product reliability problems surfaced publicly within a year, and the robotaxi business did not survive.

author: ryanwaggoner
cardQuote: This is interesting, but I cannot bring myself to believe that this is actually going to come to market.
quote: This is interesting, but I cannot bring myself to believe that this is actually going to come to market.
storyTitle: Better Place's Automated Electric Car Battery Swap Station
outcome: Better Place raised $850M, then filed for liquidation in May 2013 without reaching scale.
outcomeDetail: Better Place built battery-swap stations in Israel and Denmark and partnered with Renault, but it sold only about 1,500 cars. The company filed for liquidation in May 2013 after burning through $850 million. Its assets were later sold for a fraction of the investment.
note: ryanwaggoner's gut feeling was correct: the swap network needed automakers, governments and drivers to move in lockstep, and they never did. The demo worked; the market did not.
